planting.note: Set out divisions or container-grown plants after the last frost into gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this mat-forming species roots along its trailing stems wherever they touch soil, so give it room to spread rather than confining it to a tight pocket.

directions: Unlike the more upright blue-flowered garden cupflower, this species hugs the ground tightly and knits itself into a dense mat, making it useful as a flowering lawn substitute between stepping stones or cascading over a low wall. The rounded, cup-shaped white flowers with soft yellow centers appear in flushes from late spring through fall and are showiest when the soil stays evenly moist rather than bone dry. Shear lightly after a flowering flush to tidy the mat and encourage rebloom, and divide congested clumps every couple of years to keep the planting vigorous. It is hardy as a perennial in milder zones but is typically grown as a warm-season annual or overwintered indoors farther north.

common_name: Augusta Blue Skies Cupflower (Compact Patented Nierembergia)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after frost danger has passed into gritty, well-drained potting mix or garden soil in full sun; this patented selection was bred for earlier, more uniform flowering than seed-grown cupflower and resents soggy roots.

directions: Augusta Blue Skies is a compact, early-flowering selection bred for vegetative propagation rather than seed, giving growers a uniform crop of lavender-purple, yellow-eyed blooms that cover the trailing mound from late spring through fall. It shows good tolerance of summer heat and reported resistance to verticillium wilt, a soilborne problem that can trouble older seed strains of cupflower. Grow it in lean to average soil with sharp drainage, since the roots are quick to rot in heavy, waterlogged ground, and avoid excess nitrogen, which pushes foliage at the expense of flowers. It performs well spilling over the edge of a mixed container or hanging basket alongside heat-loving companions like calibrachoa or lantana.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants once soil has warmed after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Mandarin Orange is a compact selection best started in cell packs for even container display or sown thickly for a fast-filling bedding carpet.

directions: Mandarin Orange concentrates its bloom color into a deeper, more saturated tangerine-orange than the species type, and the small single daisies keep coming nonstop over a short, tidy mound rather than a loosely sprawling mat. It is a strong candidate for the front of a hot, dry border or the rim of a container where its low, dense habit reads as a solid ribbon of color. Because it dislikes root disturbance, sow directly where it is to bloom whenever possible, or transplant young seedlings carefully and promptly water them in. Once established it shrugs off heat and short dry spells, needing supplemental water only during prolonged drought.

common_name: Sunbini Creeping Zinnia (Compact Yellow Trailing Selection)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after frost danger has passed into well-drained soil or potting mix in full to part sun; Sunbini's mounded, self-branching habit needs no pinching to fill out a hanging basket or window box.

directions: Sunbini produces a steady flush of small, bright buttery-yellow single daisies over a naturally mounded, well-branched plant that fills out a container without pinching or deadheading. It holds up to summer heat and humidity noticeably better than many trailing bedding annuals, continuing to bloom through the hottest stretch of the season into fall. Give it a porous, well-drained mix and let the surface dry between waterings, since constantly wet roots invite rot in this drought-adapted genus. It pairs well with blue or purple trailing companions such as scaevola or trailing verbena for a high-contrast hanging basket or window box combination.

planting.note: Direct sow once the soil has warmed after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun, since this heirloom-type selection resents cool, damp conditions and transplanting disturbance.

directions: Aztec Gold bears bright golden-yellow single daisies over a long stretch from late spring through late summer, spreading into a low, sprawling mat that roots lightly where its stems touch soil. It is an older, widely available strain of creeping zinnia valued for reliable germination and a long, dependable bloom season with minimal fuss. Grow it in lean, sharply drained soil, since overly rich or wet ground produces excess foliage at the expense of flowers and increases the risk of stem rot. It thrives in heat and tolerates drought once established, making it a good choice for a hot, sunny edge, rock garden, or the front of a raised bed.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or bedding transplants after the last frost into moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Emerald Falls needs no pinching to develop its dense, tidy, cascading habit.

directions: Emerald Falls is the green-leaved counterpart to the silver-leaved dichondra trailers, with thick, softly rounded, deep-green leaves packed densely along well-branched stems that cascade over a container edge in a neat, uniform curtain. Its tighter, more symmetrical growth habit needs little grooming compared to looser silver-leaved trailers, and it tolerates more shade, making it a useful filler for baskets that get only a half-day of direct sun. It holds up well to heat once established but appreciates more consistent moisture than its silver-leaved relatives, since the broader green leaves wilt visibly during extended dry spells. Combine it with bright flowering trailers or upright bedding plants for a lush, all-season green backdrop in mixed containers.
